Compute Match — Reservation Request Lifecycle
and Status Reference
This document explains, end to end, how a reservation request moves through statuses, who triggers each
change, and which timers apply.
Two levels of status
1. Reservation request status — the status of the whole customer request.
2. Offering status — the status of each NCP’s slice ( ReservationRequestOffering ). A request sent to 3
NCPs has 3 offerings.
Do not confuse these with GPU offering status (inventory listing status: ACTIVE , PENDING_REVIEW , REJECTED ).
Reservation request statuses

Backend value UI label Meaning
Open Open Submitted; not yet routed (custom
requests start and may stay here)
AwaitingProviderAcceptance Awaiting NCP Acceptance Routed to one or more NCPs,
waiting for a response
Backend value UI label Meaning
InProcess In Process At least one NCP accepted;
negotiation under way
Contracted Contracted An NCP conﬁrmed the contract
(legacy Approved  also shows as
Contracted)
Rejected Rejected All NCPs rejected
Expired Expired Deadlines passed without action
Cancelled Cancelled Cancelled by the customer
InReview In Review Custom request being worked on by
admins
Matched Matched Custom request matched to an NCP
by admins

serviceable
The UI also shows Awaiting Provider Approval and Awaiting Customer Approval for older
proposal/counteroffer ﬂows.
Offering statuses (per NCP)
OfferingStatus : AwaitingProviderAcceptance , InProcess , Contracted , Expired , Rejected , Cancelled .
Catalog / multi-NCP ﬂow, step by step
1. Customer submits ( POST /api/v1/reservation-request ). The backend creates the request and the
customer’s ﬁrst proposal, then routes it: one offering per selected cluster (backend limit 10, UI limit 3 by
default).
2. Each offering starts as AwaitingProviderAcceptance with acceptance_expiry_date = now + 7 days . The
request becomes AwaitingProviderAcceptance.
3. Temporal starts a parent ReservationRequestWorkflow  and one child OfferingLifecycleWorkflow  per
offering. The customer gets a “request received” email; each NCP gets a magic-link email.
4. NCP accepts →  offering InProcess, contract_expiry_date = now + 45 days , NCP and customer receive
an introduction email. The ﬁrst acceptance moves the request to InProcess.
5. NCP counteroffers →  a new proposal is recorded (price-only changes update in place; material
changes create a new proposal in history).
6. NCP conﬁrms contract →  offering Contracted, an Allocation is created (status scheduled ), the
request becomes Contracted, and sibling offerings are Cancelled with “superseded” emails.
7. NCP rejects (remarks required) →  offering Rejected. If all offerings are rejected, the request is
Rejected.
8. Timers: if an NCP does not accept in 7 days →  offering Expired. If no contract in 45 days →  offering
Expired. When every offering has expired, the customer gets one consolidated expiry email and the
request becomes Expired. Reminders go out 3 days before each deadline.
9. Customer cancels →  request Cancelled; NCPs are notiﬁed.
10. Extensions: a Platform Admin (scope accept_contract_extension ) can extend acceptance or contract
deadlines by 1–200 days; this can revive an Expired offering.
                 accept               confirm contract
AwaitingProviderAcceptance ──────▶ InProcess ──────────▶ Contracted
        │   │                         │  │
  7 days│   │reject            45 days│  │reject
        ▼   ▼                         ▼  ▼
     Expired Rejected              Expired Rejected
(any non-final state) ── customer cancel / sibling contracted ──▶ Cancelled
Custom request ﬂow
A custom request has no selected cluster ( gpu_offering_id  is empty and there are no offerings).
Open ──▶ InReview ──▶ Matched
  │          │──────▶ Unserviceable
  │──────────────────▶ Matched / Unserviceable
  └── customer cancel (from Open or InReview) ──▶ Cancelled
Only admins with approver_manage_custom_reservation_request  move it forward.
Only the customer cancels.
Never returns to Open; Matched, Unserviceable and Cancelled are ﬁnal.
Custom requests never expire.
Each transition records a timestamp and optional NCP name, NCP region and comment, and emails the
customer.
Capacity rules that affect requests
Capacity windows of the same type (AVAILABLE or FUTURE) cannot partially overlap; at most one
open-ended window per type.
Availability checks use the upper bound of the tenure band (for example 2-3  years is checked as 3
years) to be conservative.
Allocations only subtract from the matching capacity type.
An optional cap ( MAX_PENDING_REQUESTS_PER_REGIONAL_CAPACITY , default 0 = unlimited) hides clusters with
too many pending requests and rejects new requests against them.
GPU count per request must be between 1 and 100,000.
Contracted price must be zero or positive and is only visible to NCPs and NVIDIA admins.
